title: Reed’s conjecture
formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy \(\chi (G)\le \lceil (\Delta (G)+1+\omega (G))/2\rceil\)?
definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from \(V(G)\) to \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; \(\chi (G)\) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and \(\Delta (G)\) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and \(\omega (G)\) is its largest possible size. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, \(\chi =\omega =1\) and \(\Delta =0\). The empty graph can be included with \(\chi =\omega =\Delta =0\), without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than \(1/2\), or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.

importance.reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.

progress.text: Reed proposes the half-average bound and proves an interpolation with some universal \(\varepsilon >0\).
Bonamy–Kelly–Nelson–Postle give stronger bounds in regimes with comparatively small clique number.
Hurley–de Joannis de Verclos–Kang report \(\varepsilon =0.119\) for large \(\Delta\); Remark 3.1 records the dependency and an \(\varepsilon =0.113\) alternative.
De Meyer and coauthors develop a distinct Kempe-recolouring analogue with additional reconfiguration obstructions.
The revised digraph analogue retains the undirected exact inequality as Conjecture 1.1 and proves only a positive-\(\varepsilon\) generalization.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.

context_blocks.text: Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so \(\chi \ge \omega\). On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most \(\Delta +1\) colours: at most \(\Delta\) colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is \(5/2\). Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient \(1/2\). Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree \(3t- 1\) and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least \(\lceil 5t/2\rceil\) colours are necessary. A universal bound \(\lceil (1- \varepsilon )(\Delta +1)+\varepsilon \omega \rceil\) with \(\varepsilon >1/2\) would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient \(\varepsilon\) in place of \(1/2\). This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report \(\varepsilon =0.119\) for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives \(\varepsilon =0.113\) using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured \(1/2\).

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by \(O(\Delta \sqrt{\log  \omega /\log  \Delta})\), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between \(\omega\) and \(\Delta\) this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is \(1/3\) because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-\(\varepsilon\) interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.

sentences: Reed's conjecture bounds chromatic number by the rounded average of maximum degree plus one and clique number.
It combines a local upper-bound scale from degree with the unavoidable coloring demand imposed by a largest clique.
The question asks whether every finite simple graph admits a coloring at this intermediate threshold.
A positive answer would give a unified quantitative relationship among three fundamental graph parameters.

The saved formulation concerns ordinary vertex coloring on unrestricted graphs, so fractional, list, directed, or recoloring variants require separate interpretation and do not automatically settle the inequality.
